title: How Molecular Gastronomy Works
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss molecular gastronomy, starting with a visit to Richard Blais's restaurant Flip Burger Boutique in Atlanta and his nitrous oxide milkshake. They cover the field's origins in the 1980s, when physical chemist Hervé This, after a failed cheese soufflé, teamed with Nicholas Kurti at Oxford to found molecular and physical gastronomy, and the field's dual aims of debunking kitchen myths and explaining cooking science. The episode explains colloids and complex dispersed systems, This's CDS shorthand (illustrated with mayonnaise), and techniques including sous vide, spherification, liquid nitrogen, and the anti-griddle. It also covers the home-kitchen tools needed, criticism of the movement, and a listener mail segment announcing the death of listener Lynn Volos, with a memorial donation suggestion.

segments.title: Opening banter and Richard Blais
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about chef Richard Blais, his Flip Burger Boutique in Atlanta, and his Top Chef All Stars run. Josh notes Blais's nitrous oxide milkshake, which was steaming, and they introduce molecular gastronomy as the episode topic.

segments.title: Origins of molecular gastronomy
segments.summary: Hervé This, a physical chemist, began studying cooking after a cheese soufflé failed in his kitchen. He partnered with Nicholas Kurti at Oxford to found molecular and physical gastronomy, and This later awarded the first doctorate in the field at the University of Paris. The field was initially controversial with chefs.

segments.title: Debunking kitchen myths and snail porridge
segments.summary: The hosts describe the field's goal of testing cooking myths, such as adding oil to pasta water, which does nothing, while a little vinegar helps keep pasta from sticking. They note the field's creative results, such as snail porridge, and the field's gradual acceptance.

segments.title: Kurti, the name change, and WD-50
segments.summary: Kurti shifted his view to art and science and the field was renamed molecular gastronomy after his death. The hosts mention Wylie Dufresne's WD-50 restaurant in New York and its ice cream bagels.

segments.title: Chemistry basics: elements, compounds, mixtures, and colloids
segments.summary: Josh explains matter as elements, compounds, or mixtures, then introduces colloids as mixtures dispersed but not dissolved, which are central to molecular gastronomy. Examples include foams like whipped cream and beer foam.

segments.title: Complex dispersed systems and This's CDS shorthand
segments.summary: Complex dispersed systems involve more than two phases, and This created a shorthand notation for them that is like a math equation. The hosts use aioli as an example and say the notation can categorize French sauces and suggest new ones. Ice cream is also a complex system of solid, liquid, gas, and colloidal states.

segments.title: Sous vide cooking
segments.summary: Sous vide involves vacuum-sealing food with spices and cooking it in a precisely controlled water bath at low temperature, retaining nutrients and juices. The hosts discuss a steak example and the equipment needed.

segments.title: Spherification
segments.summary: Spherification is a gelling reaction between calcium chloride and alginate, a seaweed-derived gum, that forms gel spheres that burst in the mouth. The hosts describe the process and an apple juice caviar example. Ferran Adrià of elBulli is credited with popularizing it.

segments.title: Anti-griddle, flash freezing, and home equipment
segments.summary: The anti-griddle cools to around negative thirty degrees Fahrenheit, and Blais has frozen mayonnaise and fried it. Flash freezing hardens a liquid's outside. The hosts then discuss the home costs for sous vide equipment, syringes, and the roughly five-thousand-dollar GastroVac.

segments.title: Liquid nitrogen and criticism of the movement
segments.summary: Blais uses liquid nitrogen for instant ice cream and for a tableside spice-collecting dish. The hosts discuss criticism that the methods are not accessible to home cooks and that the field takes soul out of cooking, and a defense that different processes can reach the same results.

segments.title: Further reading
segments.summary: The hosts point listeners to a HowStuffWorks article on molecular gastronomy and transition to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail: Lynn Volos
segments.summary: Listener Amanda writes that listener Lynn Volos has died of cancer. Amanda describes Lynn as a peacemaker in an online community and a fan of the show. The hosts suggest a donation to the Animal Rescue Fund of Mississippi in her memory, and invite listener mail.
